blocks.text: A 58-year-old man in a railway station queue suddenly falls to the floor without warning. His eyes are closed and he does not respond when you shout. Every minute without circulation reduces the chance of survival, and the first person on the scene, often a layperson or a student, determines what happens in the next few minutes.

blocks.markdown: **Cardiac arrest** is the sudden cessation of effective cardiac pumping, so that blood no longer circulates and the patient becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally. In adults it is most often caused by a primary cardiac problem. **Basic life support (BLS)** is the set of actions that keeps oxygenated blood flowing to the brain and heart until advanced help arrives: recognise arrest, call for help, start chest compressions with rescue breaths, and use an **automated external defibrillator (AED)** as soon as one is available.

blocks.title: Chain of survival
blocks.text: The **chain of survival** is the sequence of linked actions that improve survival from cardiac arrest: early recognition and call for help, early CPR, early defibrillation, and post-resuscitation care. Weakness in any link reduces the chance of survival.

blocks.markdown:
### Step 1: Recognise and call for help

1. **Make sure the scene is safe** for you, the patient and bystanders.
2. **Check responsiveness**: shake the shoulders gently and shout, "Are you all right?"
3. If there is no response, **shout for help** and **open the airway** with a head tilt and chin lift.
4. **Look, listen and feel for normal breathing** for no more than **10 seconds**. Occasional slow, noisy gasps (**agonal breathing**) are not normal breathing and are common in the first minutes of arrest.
5. If the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally, **call the emergency number** (for example 999, 112 or 911 depending on country) or ask a bystander to do so, and ask for an AED. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep going.

### Step 2: Chest compressions and rescue breaths

Place the heel of one hand on the **centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum)** and the other hand on top with fingers interlocked. With arms straight and shoulders above your hands, press down:

- **Rate**: 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
- **Depth**: 5 to 6 cm in an adult.
- **Recoil**: allow the chest to rise fully between compressions, without leaning.
- **Interruptions**: keep pauses as short as possible.

If trained and willing, give **two rescue breaths** after every **30 compressions** (ratio 30:2). Tilt the head, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over the patient's and blow for about one second, watching for the chest to rise. If you cannot or do not want to give breaths, give continuous compressions.

blocks.latex: \text{compression fraction} = \frac{\text{time spent compressing}}{\text{total time of the resuscitation attempt}}
blocks.caption: Higher fractions mean less time without blood flow.

blocks.title: How long do 30 compressions take?
blocks.prompt: A rescuer compresses at 120 compressions per minute. How many seconds does one set of 30 compressions take?

steps.text: Convert the rate to compressions per second: $120 \div 60 = 2$ compressions per second.
Divide the number of compressions by the rate to get time.
Check the result against the guideline range: at 100 per minute the same 30 compressions would take 18 s, so 15 s lies at the fast end of the range, which is acceptable.

blocks.caption: Key adult BLS parameters (international consensus; local guidelines differ slightly)
rows: Centre of the chest, lower half of the sternum
As few and as brief as possible

blocks.title: Compression fraction in a cycle
blocks.prompt: In one cycle a rescuer gives 30 compressions at 120 per minute and then pauses 5 seconds to give two breaths. What is the compression fraction of this cycle?

steps.text: Time compressing: 30 compressions at 2 per second is 15 s.
Total cycle time: 15 s compressing plus 5 s pause is 20 s.
Interpretation: 75% of the time blood is being circulated; longer pauses lower the fraction.

blocks.markdown:
### Step 3: Use an automated external defibrillator

An **AED** analyses the heart rhythm and advises a shock only for **shockable rhythms** (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia). It will not shock a flat line (asystole) or an organised rhythm without a pulse; those need CPR.

1. **Switch on** the AED as soon as it arrives and follow the voice or visual prompts. Continue CPR while the pads are attached.
2. **Attach the pads** to bare, dry skin: one below the right collarbone to the right of the sternum, the other on the left side of the chest below the armpit.
3. **Stand clear** while the AED analyses, and make sure nobody is touching the patient.
4. If a shock is advised, check again that everyone is clear and **press the shock button** (or wait for automatic delivery).
5. **Resume CPR immediately** for two minutes, or until the AED prompts again, without waiting to check for a pulse.

blocks.title: Do not wait for the AED to start CPR
blocks.text: Start compressions immediately. Never delay CPR to look for an AED, and keep compressing until the pads are attached and the AED says to stop.

blocks.title: Safety around the shock
blocks.text: Nobody must touch the patient during analysis or shock delivery. Move the patient away from standing water and do not use pads over a visible implanted device or medication patch; place them elsewhere.

items: Check response, shout for help, open the airway.
Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Call the emergency number and ask for an AED.
Start 30 compressions then 2 breaths, and apply the AED as soon as it arrives.

points: Recognise cardiac arrest: unresponsive and not breathing normally (gasping does not count), then call for help and an AED.
Compress the centre of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute and 5 to 6 cm deep with full recoil, using a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
Follow AED prompts exactly: attach pads, stand clear for analysis and shock, then resume CPR at once.
Minimise interruptions: a high compression fraction means more time with blood flow.

questions.stem: A man is found unresponsive and is only making occasional slow, noisy gasps about once every 20 seconds. What should the rescuer conclude?

options.text: He is in cardiac arrest because agonal gasps are not normal breathing
He is breathing normally and should be placed in the recovery position
He is asleep and should be woken gently
He has a pulse and needs only oxygen

questions.correctOptionText: He is in cardiac arrest because agonal gasps are not normal breathing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: agonal breathing is a sign of arrest, not of adequate breathing.
distractorRationale.b: The recovery position is for those who are breathing normally.
distractorRationale.d: BLS does not depend on a pulse check by lay rescuers.

questions.explanation: Agonal breathing is a reflex that can occur in the first minutes after the heart stops. It must not delay calling for help and starting CPR.

questions.stem: What is the recommended compression to ventilation ratio for adult CPR performed by a trained rescuer?

options.text: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
15 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
2 compressions to 30 breaths

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 30:2 is the standard adult ratio.
distractorRationale.b: 15:2 is an older or paediatric two-rescuer ratio, not the adult standard.

questions.explanation: Adult BLS uses 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. Long runs of compressions maintain coronary perfusion and the breaths are limited to brief pauses.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes chest compression technique in an adult?

options.text: 5 to 6 cm depth, 100 to 120 per minute, allowing full chest recoil
2 to 3 cm depth, 60 to 80 per minute, leaning on the chest
5 to 6 cm depth, 140 to 160 per minute, with short recoil
8 to 10 cm depth, 100 to 120 per minute, one hand only

questions.correctOptionText: 5 to 6 cm depth, 100 to 120 per minute, allowing full chest recoil

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these values match the consensus recommendation.
distractorRationale.b: Too shallow, too slow and leaning prevents venous return to the heart.
distractorRationale.c: Rate too fast, which reduces filling time.
distractorRationale.d: Excessive depth can injure; both hands are used.

questions.explanation: A depth of 5 to 6 cm and a rate of 100 to 120 per minute provide adequate blood flow. Allowing full recoil lets the heart refill between compressions.

questions.stem: A rescuer has attached AED pads to a 70-year-old woman in cardiac arrest. The AED announces, "Analysing rhythm, do not touch the patient." What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Stop touching the patient and make sure everyone is clear
Continue compressions so that blood flow is not interrupted
Check for a carotid pulse
Remove the pads and restart the AED

questions.correctOptionText: Stop touching the patient and make sure everyone is clear

distractorRationale.a: Correct: movement or touch can disturb the analysis.
distractorRationale.b: Compressions create artefact and may prevent correct analysis.
distractorRationale.c: A pulse check by a lay rescuer delays treatment.
distractorRationale.d: Removing the pads interrupts the analysis.

questions.explanation: The AED needs a clean signal to interpret the rhythm, so nobody should touch the patient during analysis. Once the AED advises, follow its next prompt immediately.

questions.stem: True or false: an AED will advise a shock for asystole (a flat line).

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: AEDs shock only shockable rhythms, which are ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Asystole is not shockable, so CPR must continue.

questions.stem: After a shock has been delivered by an AED to a collapsed 64-year-old man, what is the next action?

options.text: Restart chest compressions immediately
Wait 2 minutes and then check for a pulse
Switch off the AED and wait for the ambulance
Give a second shock at once

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CPR resumes at once for two minutes or until the AED prompts.
distractorRationale.c: The AED must stay attached and switched on.
distractorRationale.d: The AED decides when the next shock is advised after the next analysis.

questions.explanation: After a shock the heart is usually not yet pumping effectively, so compressions are restarted at once. The AED will re-analyse after the next two-minute cycle.

questions.stem: A rescuer delivers 30 chest compressions at a steady rate of 100 compressions per minute. How long, in seconds, do the 30 compressions take?
questions.explanation: At 100 compressions per minute the rate is 100/60 compressions per second, so 30 compressions take 30 divided by 1.667 = 18 seconds. This is within the guideline range of 100 to 120 per minute.

questions.stem: A rescuer performs cycles of 30 compressions at 120 per minute followed by a 6-second pause for two breaths. Calculate the compression fraction of one cycle as a decimal between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: 30 compressions at 2 per second take 15 s. The cycle is 15 + 6 = 21 s, so the fraction is 15 divided by 21 = 0.714. Longer pauses reduce this fraction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man collapses in a shopping centre and is unresponsive. Describe the sequence by which a first responder recognises cardiac arrest and activates the emergency response.
markingGuide: Checks response by shaking and shouting
Shouts for help and opens the airway
Looks, listens and feels for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Recognises that agonal gasps are not normal breathing
Calls the emergency number and asks for an AED
questions.explanation: The key is a rapid, ordered assessment with a time limit on the breathing check. Calling early and sending someone for an AED improve the chance of early defibrillation.

questions.stem: Explain why minimising interruptions to chest compressions matters, and describe how a rescuer should use an AED, starting from its arrival at the scene.
markingGuide: Interruptions stop coronary and cerebral perfusion
Continue CPR while the AED is prepared
Attach pads to bare dry skin in the correct positions
Stand clear during analysis and shock
Resume CPR immediately after the shock
questions.explanation: Every pause removes blood flow to the heart and brain, and coronary perfusion pressure takes time to rebuild. An AED is used by following its prompts while keeping hands-off time to the minimum.
